metadata.key_test: Colonial-institutional ENGINEERING as a fragmentation driver: two populations with DIFFERENT colonial-institutional legacies (British common-law Southern Cameroons + French civil-law Cameroun, merged 1961) compressed into one state -> does low-moderate P1 (0.365) + high INSTITUTIONAL heterogeneity produce fragmentation pressure along the institutional fault line (the 2016-17 Anglophone crisis / 'Ambazonia' declaration), and does Safeguard G Tier 1 (military suppression) DELAY-but-not-RESOLVE -> ongoing unresolved instability (MI 0.517 -> 0.384)? The Anglophone NW/SW regions have no standalone WGI; analyzed via Cameroon + qualitative evidence.
metadata.notes: Reference-based single-entity record; Cameroon carries real MI v2 re-scores. 2016 Anglophone protests -> 2017 'Ambazonia' declaration -> ongoing armed conflict; scored ~2015 (pre) vs 2024. Fills the Francophone-Africa gap and isolates colonial-institutional (legal-tradition) heterogeneity rather than the ethnic/religious heterogeneity of Nigeria/Biafra (case12). Replaces the original Ethiopia-federal proposal (overlap with cases 8/11).

pre_event.event_description: On the eve of the 2016 Anglophone protests, Cameroon is a single state engineered from two different colonial-institutional inheritances: the formerly British-administered Southern Cameroons (common law, English-language education and administration) joined the formerly French-administered Cameroun (civil law, French institutions) in 1961. Decades of centralization eroded the federal/bicultural settlement; by 2015 Anglophone lawyers and teachers were protesting the imposition of Francophone legal and educational norms on the NW and SW regions -- a grievance located precisely on the institutional fault line.

context.neighbor_details: Borders Nigeria, whose own Anglophone identity and porous border provide an exogenous cross-border dimension (Safeguard D) to the Anglophone separatist movement; Boko Haram pressure in the Far North is a separate northern stress.
context.fragmentation_mechanism: colonial-institutional engineering -- two legal/administrative traditions (British common law + French civil law) compressed into one centralized state; fragmentation pressure along the institutional fault line

Cameroon.notes: Inputs resolved live via mi.datasource (country_ref + year). WGI 2025-anchored 0-100. Cameroon: long-personalist authoritarian rule with low-moderate P1 (0.365). The key structural variable is INSTITUTIONAL heterogeneity (two colonial legal traditions) within one centralized state -- distinct from the ethnic/religious heterogeneity of Nigeria/Biafra (case12). The Anglophone NW/SW regions have no separate WGI; analyzed via the parent state plus qualitative evidence.

Cameroon.outcome_summary: Confirmed directionally and in FORM. The 2016 lawyer/teacher protests escalated to a 2017 'Ambazonia' independence declaration and a sustained armed insurgency in the NW/SW regions, met by military suppression (Safeguard G Tier 1). The conflict remained unresolved through 2024 (thousands killed, hundreds of thousands displaced; OCHA reported millions in need). MI deteriorated 0.517 -> 0.384, dropping from Tier 3 to Tier 4; P1 fell 0.365 -> 0.351 and cohesion P5 fell 0.474 -> 0.305. No recognized successor state -- an unresolved, suppressed de facto contested zone, exactly the predicted Tier-1 'delay-not-resolve' outcome.

conflict unresolved through 2024; no recognized secession

analysis.overall_assessment: Directional confirmation in both magnitude and FORM: low P1 plus dual colonial-institutional legacies produced fragmentation pressure precisely along the Anglophone institutional fault line, and Safeguard G Tier 1 military suppression delayed without resolving it -- MI fell from Tier 3 to Tier 4 with the conflict still active in 2024.
analysis.what_this_case_uniquely_reveals: Colonial-institutional ENGINEERING is an isolable fragmentation driver: when two populations with different LEGAL/administrative traditions (common law vs civil law) are compressed into one centralized state, fragmentation pressure forms along the institutional fault line itself -- a cleaner test of institutional-legacy heterogeneity than the ethnically noisy Nigeria/Biafra (case12). It also sharpens the Safeguard G/I contrast: Cameroon's Tier-1 military suppression WITHOUT an autonomy backstop yields ongoing unresolved instability, the mirror image of Aceh's (case35) autonomy-with-backstop resolution.
analysis.baseline_impact: None; adds the Francophone-Africa case, isolates institutional-legacy heterogeneity as a complexity variable, and adds a Safeguard G Tier 1 confirmation (with Fiji case33 / Sudan case50). Replaces the original Ethiopia-federal proposal to avoid overlap with cases 8/11.
